{#cn87} # Discussion

{#nzs0} The current study evaluated the general awareness of CKD among female non-medical university students in Riyadh. The findings of this study show that female university students in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, who are not medical professionals have unsatisfactory knowledge level regarding CKD’s general knowledge, where only 53.2% had adequate knowledge. Our findings fell a little bit short of a study done in Saudi Arabia [@w:w17] where 57.1% had adequate knowledge. there could be a reason for the variations in knowledge levels between our study and their study. One hypothesis is that compared to the university students in the current study, the participants in their study came from a wider variety of backgrounds.

{#y5u1} Moreover, our findings suggest that there is no significant association between sociodemographic characteristics and knowledge of CKD, but some variations were found, and we think that the following hypotheses may explain theses variations. For example, we think that our unsatisfactory level of knowledge might be related to our sample age group, since more than half of our participants were young adults and CKD is not common in this age.

{#igbg} # Introduction

{#clea} According to National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), kidney failure is a medical illness in which the kidneys are no longer able to function at levels that are sufficient to filter the blood’s waste products. It’s also referred to as chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) [@w:w1]. Acute renal failure (ARF) which manifests quickly and may resolve, is distinguished from chronic renal failure (CRF), which manifest gradually and frequently becomes irreversible [@w:w2].

{#e5if} CKD is a growing global health concern that significantly affects morbidity and mortality rates worldwide [@w:w3]. The prevalence of CKD has steadily increased over the past few decades due to the rising incidence of risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, and obesity [@w:w4]. In Saudi Arabia, CKD poses a particular challenge, with the country witnessing a steady rise in the number of patients suffering from end-stage renal disease (ESRD) [@w:w5]. Despite the severity of CKD and its associated complications, public awareness regarding the disease, especially in non-medical populations, remains insufficient . Studies have shown that early detection and lifestyle modifications can significantly delay the progression of CKD and improve patient outcomes [@w:w6]. ops.markdown: In the present study, a key finding was that CKD knowledge was unrelated to income: participants with the highest income had the lowest knowledge levels, at 51.2%, which may reflect better healthcare access and screening among the well-off.
